Abstract

AI tools now help people write, program, analyze data, and design, and many also aim to help people learn through that work. What such a tool gives a person to think with varies: a generated explanation, criteria for judging alternatives, an editable plan, a record of earlier choices. We call these designed structures with task meaning semantic scaffolding. We reviewed 4,511 AI-involved papers from 40 venues (2019–2026), together with theories and empirical studies of how support works, and synthesized a design space of 5 mechanism families and 18 categories. Compared with papers on earlier AI, generative-AI papers more often concern producing artifacts and more often give people control over what the system does, after adjusting for venue and year. What a person can edit matters: the task specification, the AI's interpretation of it, the criteria, or the result. Designs also differ in whether people construct a representation, reason with supplied material, or judge proposed results. Studies that measure learning report gains and costs together: CodeVoyager raised closed-book comprehension without a completion advantage, and required reflection cut completed practice from 3.4 to 2.0 problems in a fixed time. The design space gives researchers named alternatives to build and test.

Keywords: Semantic scaffolding, learning, human–AI interaction, external cognition, landscape review, interface mechanisms

1 Introduction

A writer asks Luminate for story ideas. Instead of one draft, the system proposes dimensions along which ideas can differ and fills each with options [122]. The dimensions help the writer survey the possibilities and compare ideas. They are also generated, and a generated dimension can miss what matters to this writer. The writer now judges two things: the ideas, and the structure offered for judging them.

This is the design problem we study. AI tools increasingly supply the structures people think with, not only the content they produce: criteria, examples, relations between concepts, plans, and records of earlier choices. We use semantic scaffolding to describe designed structures with task meaning that a person inspects or acts through. The term joins two lines of work. Scaffolding research asks how support lets a learner do what they could not yet do alone [136, 102]; cognitive-artifact research asks how representations change the task a person performs [94]. The assistance dilemma and ICAP add that what support supplies, and what it leaves for the learner to do, shapes what people learn [66, 28].

Broad labels such as feedback, reflection, and user control hide the choices that matter. Editing a generated answer differs from correcting how the AI interpreted the request before it answered. A learner's account prepared for a coach differs from a simulated learner used to rehearse coaching. We map these choices across domains such as programming, writing, data analysis, and design, connect them to the work people do, and compare what studies found when the choices were tested.

We reviewed papers from 40 HCI, AI, and learning venues published from 2019 to 2026. Working with language models, we screened 35,480 titles and abstracts, selected 7,372 papers for full-text review, and analyze 4,511 in which AI is part of the system or study and a person inspects or acts through a designed structure. A second body of work, theories and empirical studies of how support works and when it helps, gives the comparisons we use to interpret designs; it includes studies without AI. We ask:

  • RQ1. What work and human capabilities does semantic-scaffolding research support, and how has this focus changed from 2019 to 2026?
  • RQ2. How is semantic scaffolding designed, and what does existing evidence show about its support for performance and learning?

We contribute:

  1. a design space of semantic scaffolding in AI-assisted work, with 5 mechanism families and 18 categories, each illustrated by named systems;
  2. an account of what people can inspect and change in these designs (the specification, the AI's interpretation, the criteria, or the result) and of how support passes between learners, peers, teachers, and coaches;
  3. a comparison of the consequences studies report for performance and learning, tied to the design alternatives they tested.

2 Background

2.1 Scaffolding and Cognitive Artifacts

Scaffolding began as an account of tutoring: a tutor takes over the parts of a task a learner cannot yet manage, so the learner can do the rest [136]. Developmental scaffolding responds to the learner, reduces help as the learner improves, and hands over responsibility [126]. Reiser separates structuring a task from problematizing it, drawing attention to what the learner must reason about [107], and inquiry-support guidelines turn these ideas into design [106]. Support can also be spread across people, artifacts, and tools [102, 10]. Pea argues that support meant to stay should be kept apart from scaffolding that fades. Sherin et al. extend the metaphor into a comparative account of scaffolded activity [116], and Puntambekar and Hübscher warn that calling a tool a scaffold does not make its help responsive to the learner [105].

Cognitive artifacts are support meant to stay. Norman uses the term for designed devices that store, display, or transform information for a task [94]. He distinguishes what the person and the artifact accomplish together from how the artifact changes the person's task: a checklist moves work into preparing, consulting, and interpreting the list. The same content supports different operations when it is arranged differently [146, 112]. People also change the world to help themselves reason [64], and several representations can aid understanding while adding the work of coordinating them [2].

We use semantic scaffolding for designed structures with task meaning—concepts, relations, examples, criteria—that a person inspects or acts through, whether they fade or stay. Zong et al. use the term for an LLM technique that explains domain groupings of data to blind and low-vision readers [151]; we use it more broadly. Keeping the two kinds of support apart matters for evaluation: performance with a tool and capability without it are different outcomes, and only the second shows growth toward independence [102, 105].

2.2 Representations in AI Interfaces

Recent design spaces describe these representational choices directly. Min et al. separate an abstraction's schema from its representation and examine granularity, presentation, and transformation [89]. Kim et al. organize how generative interfaces elicit preferences along six axes, including when a request appears and which part of an artifact it concerns [62]. Systems show the range. In Graphologue, selecting a concept extends a diagram with related concepts and links the person can follow and question [58]. In AI Chains, intermediate steps expose how a problem, a suggestion, and drafted feedback connect, and people can change each step [139]. In HaLLMark, a highlight marks authorship and links a passage to the prompt that produced it [51]. A cue can show that an action exists without showing what it does [95]: in Codestrates v2, a file-like tree organized code, and its order also governed execution, which one participant discovered only in use [18].

People and technology change together. Mackay describes users who repurposed email filters, built to sort messages before reading, into tools for filing them afterwards; the developers then supported both uses [83]. Interfaces have long adapted controls to a person's abilities [44, 134]. LLMs add support generated during use: diagrams that grow during exploration [58], views people recompose [88], and representations generated as tasks change [23]. A generated view can perform an operation, expose relations, and become the control for the next step. The design questions are who builds it, who can revise it, and what work its use adds or removes.

2.3 Offloading and Control in AI-Assisted Work

Distributed cognition treats people, tools, and artifacts as one cognitive system [49]. The extended-mind argument counts reliably consulted resources as part of memory [31], and material structures hold relations otherwise kept in mind [57]. Offloading changes what people retain: expected access to information shifts memory toward where to find it [119], and automation can leave operators with the hardest cases and little practice [8]. Mixed-initiative interaction combines automation with direct manipulation [52]. Interactive machine learning makes the user–system loop the object of design [3], explainable-AI frameworks separate understanding, trust, debugging, and decision support [92], and teaming and learning-support research adds capability and transfer [22, 46]. Because people trade accuracy against effort [101], making some operations easy also changes strategies. Generative systems that expose prompts, plans, alternatives, and evidence [65, 122, 138, 24] also produce task criteria and explanations on demand, so people may need to check the guidance as well as the answer.

2.4 Landscape Reviews and Design Spaces

Design spaces organize recurring choices and the criteria for weighing them [84], and how they are drawn shapes what designers explore [14, 72]. HCI landscapes relate creativity support tools to practice and evaluation [40], organize traces of creative activity [48], and examine generative tools in artists' work [65]. Citeology, Royal Constellations, and HCI Research Trails make citation relationships navigable [87, 19, 91]; we also record what a cited source does in a paper: frame it, explain a mechanism, shape a design, or provide a measure.

Earlier syntheses relate contingent support and learner activity to learning [126, 11]. Self-explanation research identifies practice exposure and redundant prompting as conditions that matter [109]. The assistance dilemma and ICAP frame when to give help and what engagement it invites [66, 28], and expertise reversal and desirable difficulties qualify what a practice result means [60, 15]. Krakauer distinguishes artifacts that leave capability behind when removed from those whose advantage lasts only while they are in use [67]. Human–AI guidelines already address intelligibility and correction [4]. Our addition is a comparison of concrete design choices across domains, linked to the activity each asks of people and to what studies measured when they tested it.

3 Methods

We reviewed two bodies of work (Figure 2). Stream 1 is a systematic corpus of AI-involved systems and studies from fixed venues and years; it supplies the designs we map. Stream 2 collects theories and empirical studies of how support works, including studies without AI; we interpret the designs against it. The two are counted separately. Scoping-review guidance shaped selection, extraction, and reporting [6, 73, 124], and earlier HCI landscape reviews shaped the venue frame and synthesis [40, 48].

3.1 Literature Review

3.1.1 Venues

Stream 1 covers 40 venues in HCI, design and creativity, visualization, graphics, learning and education, software engineering, and AI and language, published from 2019 to 2026 (Figure 3). Papers are dated by their version of record; the selection figure, the design space, and the trend figures cover papers published by 16 July 2026. Ineligible publication types were excluded by rule, and citation counts played no part.

3.1.2 Screening

Two language models separately screened the 35,480 records with an abstract; the 2,498 without one were not screened. Their verdicts, a review of their disagreements, and (for the first reading list) PDF availability determined the 7,372 records selected for full-text reading. One model read each paper and recorded, with passages and pages, whether it met the criteria.

The AI requirement was added partway through full-text reading, so three separate model passes rechecked the 1,154 earlier cards that left the question open. A paper left the corpus only when all three found no AI, with low uncertainty and a quoted passage (492 cards). The corpus holds 4,511 papers, and 1,076 of them form a learning subset: their support has a documented learning purpose, or the study examines its learning consequences. Another 474 papers without AI form a labeled comparison set outside the systematic corpus counts; the text marks any it uses as an example.

3.1.3 Inclusion Criteria

Stream 1 includes a paper when three conditions hold, at screening and at full text (Figure 4): AI is part of the system or the study; the paper implements or studies a designed structure with task meaning; and a person inspects or acts through that structure. AI is part of a paper when an AI system is built, used, evaluated, or simulated (including Wizard-of-Oz systems presented as AI), or when AI is what the study designs, explains, or labels. Rewording a chatbot's replies (hedges, tone, length) is not a designed structure. Workshop templates, cards, storyboards, and probes used to elicit views count only when the paper builds and evaluates them as its contribution. Reviews, surveys, and meta-analyses go to Stream 2. A design can qualify without a user study; its benefits then count as intended uses, not measured effects. Learning purpose, measured outcomes, adaptation, fading, and the transfer of responsibility are recorded but do not decide inclusion.

3.1.4 Theories and Empirical Studies

Stream 2 gathers theories, design principles, and empirical findings about how support works. Its sources came from database searches, backward and forward citation snowballing [135], and reviews found in Stream 1, and every source received the same full-text assessment of relevance and support. Of 795 candidate works, we read 543 in full and excluded 31 for recorded reasons, such as falling outside the review questions or appearing in a questionable venue. The analysis uses the remaining 512 sources and their 2,867 claims. Books, foundational theory, null findings, and studies without AI are eligible.

3.2 Analysis

3.2.1 What We Recorded

A model read each full text and filled a structured evidence card, quoting the passages and pages behind its entries.[note]Evidence cards: mechanism, theory-lineage, and knowledge-claim cards. Scientific-document benchmarks and expert-assisted literature mining offer precedents for such passage-linked records [127, 132]. The Stream 1 unit is a mechanism, an operation involving a designed structure with task meaning: AI Chains' workflow overview and its step editor are two mechanisms [139]. For each mechanism, the card records what the interface represents, how and when it presents that meaning, and what people can do. It also records how the work changed, what the tool took over and what the person kept, and how the design was evaluated: comparison, measures, duration, participants, and results. A second card records how the paper uses each cited source: to frame a problem, explain a mechanism, motivate the design, inform a measure, critique an approach, or in passing. The Stream 2 unit is a knowledge claim, a finding or theoretical argument about how support works, for whom, and when; each card holds one to eight claims with their evidence, conditions, and limits. Missing information is recorded as not reported or unclear, and author claims, measured results, and reviewer inferences stay apart (fields in Appendix A).

3.2.2 Building the Design Space

Closed fields take predefined values, such as whether learning was measured and for how long; open fields describe mechanisms and human work in each paper's terms. We merged the 142,877 open-field observations into 1,290 codes and grouped these into 223 categories and 92 families across 18 fields (Appendix A.3). Each grouping links to its observations, so the grouping and the assignments can be checked separately [54]. The mechanism field's hierarchy is the design space: 5 families and 18 categories (Section 5; codebook in Appendix B). For the four-function view (Figure 12), we assigned each of the 110 mechanism codes to the functions it serves; exploring alternatives serves both representing and evaluating.

We built the vocabulary from the cards completed by 28 August 2026 and coded later cards with it. The design-space counts describe the 2,847 papers of that first set still in the corpus (2,891 for the closed fields); the annual and technology figures draw on the 4,086 papers with usable coding (Appendix A.6). A paper counts once per category, however many mechanisms it has. We classified each paper's AI as generative or traditional AI/ML by the technology it used, not its year, and adjusted technology comparisons for year and venue, since venue mix alone can create differences (Appendix D).

3.2.3 Comparing Designs and Studies

We used the codes to find cases and the source passages to compare them. For each question, we compared the task, the representation supplied, the actions available, the reported use, and the assessed consequence, recording contrary and unclear cases beside supporting ones. We chose examples that fit a mechanism, varying domain and year; citation counts mattered only after fit. We retrieved prior findings and counterexamples through the seven fields coded on Stream 2 claims, such as the form of support and a claim's conditions. The lineage cards trace how a cited theory or finding entered a design or a measure (Section 5.5); reference lists and citation counts come from Semantic Scholar (Appendix A.9.2).

For study results, each contrast keeps its population, comparator, outcome, timing, and the assistance available during assessment, and positive, mixed, null, harmful, and unmeasured results stay distinct. A whole-system result is credited to the whole system, and a learning claim counts as tested only when a study measured learning or transfer. We sorted outcomes into process, artifact, and learning, each assessed by the study or reported by participants (Section 5.6). We did not pool effects across studies (Section 8).

3.2.4 Checking the Coding

Scripts checked the cards' required fields and matched their quotations against the source text, and quotations the text layer could not match were checked against page images; counts and plots are computed from the saved data. To test the open-code grouping, a separate model pass coded 1,571 extracted observations in six fields with the existing codes hidden. Agreement was low (adjusted Rand index .079 to .445), and the blind pass grouped more coarsely in five of the six fields (Appendix A.4). The mechanism vocabulary gained 12 codes across the 1,754 papers read after it was built (Appendix E).

3.3 AI Use Disclosure

We used language models to screen, read, and code papers, group codes, develop and critique the cross-case comparisons, write analysis code, and draft and revise text, tables, and figures. Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol screened titles and abstracts. GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and Claude Opus 5.5 read the full texts and wrote the Stream 1 cards; Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol wrote the Stream 2 cards; Claude Opus 5.5 ran the three-pass AI check. Claude Opus 5 merged labels into codes, and model-assisted review, including Claude Fable 5.1, grouped the codes into categories and families. GPT-6 Sol linked card evidence for the cross-case comparisons, and GPT-6 Astra developed and critiqued them. GPT-6 Astra, working through Codex, drafted the merged manuscript, and Claude Opus 5.5 revised it. Prompts and run records are kept. The authors set the research questions, scope, criteria, and card formats, directed the synthesis, and are responsible for its conclusions; people have not yet checked the coding or the cross-case interpretations (Section 8).

4 Findings: Workflows and Capabilities

AI can supply material for a person to work from or produce the artifact the person will judge. That difference changes the work left to people. We first examine the shift toward generation, then distinguish what people compose, check, and decide, and finally follow support across learners, teachers, and collaborators. The activity map in Figure 5 identifies the work being supported; Figure 7 separates contributions from tools and people.

4.1 Work represented and changes in research attention

CorpusStudio and ABScribe both support writing, but supply different starting points. CorpusStudio retrieves examples and patterns from prior writing for authors to interpret before composing their own prose [32]. ABScribe generates alternative passages that authors keep, edit, and compare [108]. One supplies material to write from; the other supplies passages to select and revise. The broader technology comparison locates this distinction across the review.

GenAI moves generation to the tool. In 2,119 papers from 2019–2025 with coded delegated work, the tool generates the artifact in 19.3% of GenAI and 1.9% of traditional AI/ML papers (+16.6 points after adjusting for year and venue; 95% CI 12.7 to 20.5), and it more often generates responses and revisions (+9.4). Analysis moves the other way: the tool less often calculates and models (-11.5), evaluates and classifies (-9.7), or compares and finds patterns (-6.7) (Appendix D.2).

The contrast concerns the work assigned to tools; it does not establish a change in the field's domain mix. Within venues, no annual change in a domain's share from 2019 to 2025 survived correction for multiple tests (Table 12). The quantitative pool contains 4,086 AI-involved paper groups; each comparison uses the subset with the required coding and technology classification. GenAI includes earlier generative models and generative hybrids; traditional AI/ML appears in every year. GenAI becomes the majority from 2024 (Figure 6). Technology comparisons omit 639 papers with unresolved technology, and 2026 is partial because papers were collected in July.

The paired workflow figure uses 2,390 papers with an activity code and assigned technology. Allocation, supplied support, reported outcomes, and study-description codes remain separate: faster work, for example, does not establish automation. Appendix D gives annual domain and activity distributions and the counts behind each share (Figure 55 and Figure 56). A paper can support several activities.

4.2 Delegating work while retaining judgment

Generating more of an artifact leaves open a second question: what enables the person to judge and act on it? The writing contrast above separates composition from selection and revision. Other designs leave people to check execution, interpret an explanation, or authorize an action.

Figure 7 makes this division of work explicit. A tool can compose material while the person judges its fit, revises it, or checks its evidence. Learning and reflection are distinct from supervising the system: either may be described without the other. These distinctions locate the action to examine in a design; the outcome comparisons later in the paper establish what was measured.

Norman separates what a system accomplishes from the activity of the person using it [94]. In the reviewed interfaces, composing a passage, choosing a criterion, inspecting execution, and deciding whether to keep an alternative are separate operations, and designs divide them differently.

Different references support different checks. A proposed result can be checked against executed values, retrieved examples, the system's interpretation of an action, or a generated forecast. Leap shows the values that generated code produces as it runs [39]; CorpusStudio retrieves examples from a writing corpus [32]; ONYX shows how it interpreted an action the user taught it [111]; and Rehearsal simulates how a conversation partner might respond [114]. Each grounds a different judgment. A simulated response is material for rehearsal, not a validated prediction of what a particular person will say. A corpus supplies precedents, but its incomplete coverage cannot show that an idea is new.

A reference helps only when people notice and use it. ONYX's full interface improved script accuracy, yet users missed or wrongly dismissed 44.8% of its follow-up questions [111]. Leap's live values did not significantly change validation success compared with a condition in which people could still run the code themselves [39]. A design therefore has to name the error a person should catch, the information that reveals it, and the response that would show the check worked.

ExPeerience shows that generation need not turn learners into passive checkers: it uses AI to create problem contexts, tables, and explanations but leaves writing the SQL solution to the learner [149].

4.3 Coordination and opportunities to learn

Support can pass through another person whose judgment remains necessary. In entrepreneurship coaching, the novice describes a project and selects risks; the interface gives the mentor selected and omitted risks with source traces to prepare a meeting [55]. HTCT instead turns tutor discourse into analytics that a coach selects and discusses with the tutor [17]. One representation carries a person's expressed priorities; the other supplies an analysis of their activity. The immediate interface user, contributor, and intended beneficiary can be different people.

These arrangements require following what crosses roles. The entrepreneurship study observed eleven novices and one mentor in real meetings, with changes in plans and diagnoses. Coaches chose whether to use HTCT. The study followed their tutors' practice for seven weeks across early, delayed, and no-access groups. The entrepreneurship study observed coaching meetings; HTCT tracked the tutors' subsequent practice. Rehearsal instead lets the person practice conflict responses with a generated counterpart [114]. The distinction is between preparing a real exchange and rehearsing a possible one.

A shared representation does not guarantee a response. In eaSEL, a child's reflective artifact can be shown to a parent with a prompt about the parent's own experience, but the evaluation did not observe the whole parent–child exchange the paper proposes [115]. QMaps, a system without AI, makes the participation issue concrete. Students create questions, link prerequisites, and justify those links. Incorrect links sometimes revealed copied content that students did not understand, while students preferred adding their own questions to revising others' work [141]. Exposing reasoning could reveal a difficulty without ensuring that anyone addressed it.

The social arrangement can also change when software supplies feedback. BrailleBlocks makes a child's construction interpretable to a sighted parent who can offer hints [42]. In WriteAid (Stream 2), some recurring questions became less visible to a teacher when pupils sought software feedback, while the teacher gained time to circulate and new peer conversations occurred [93]. These cases turn on who has the information needed to help and how their role changes when software intervenes.

Educator-facing support can also target different work. VizProg users diagnosed learners' code and selected feedback during a classroom replay, but that feedback was not delivered to students [145]. M-Powering Teachers supplied mentors with feedback about their own talk; randomized access increased their uptake of students' contributions and reduced their share of talk [33]. QLens lets designers inspect prospective feedback: one recommended path derived from successful traces was judged unsuitable as direct feedback for students [140].

These cases assess diagnosis, teaching practice, and feedback suitability. M-Powering's result concerns the ongoing feedback package; its study did not record time on the feedback page or directly assess student learning. Educators can themselves be the intended learners. QLens adds a different qualification: a path students completed successfully can still be unsuitable as instruction. Following the recipient's response is therefore central to understanding what the shared representation accomplishes.

The next section turns to the interface mechanisms that organize this work and to what evaluations of those designs show.

Explore prior knowledge: reference map and documented source uses →

5 Findings: Mechanism Taxonomy

The work described above can be supported through different interface choices: exposing a reason, organizing alternatives, letting a person change them, guiding a next step, or sharing an interpretation. The 5 mechanism families and 18 categories organize these choices. We first map the mechanisms and their prevalence, then examine how they work together through an iterative activity. Comparisons of revision, judgment, and practice show what particular designs make possible. Prior learning research explains some of their rationales; the final subsections examine what their evaluations establish.

5.1 Mechanism families

A mechanism pairs an operation with its form: a constraint can express a goal, an authored rule, or an adjustable threshold. Figure 9 organizes these forms, and Figure 10 compares their prevalence across technologies; a paper can use several. Table 17 counts the papers in each category and how many of them concern or measure learning, and the category maps in Appendix C.1 lead to particular mechanisms and their source papers.

The families describe different ways to support a decision. The organization and comparison family supplies alternatives, relationships, and histories. Graphologue turns text into entities and links [58]; Crystalline gathers options, criteria, and evidence from the pages a developer reads into a comparison table whose cells lead back to their sources [75]. The guidance and feedback family supplies recommendations, questions, and task structure. OATutor selects practice and reveals hints [100], while WithYou shortens the pauses it inserts into speech as a learner's shadowing improves [147]; revealing more help and reducing help are different interventions.

The explanation and visibility family exposes sources, rationale, or state. HaLLMark traces copied LLM text to its prompts but relies on writers to mark the passages they consider AI-influenced [51]; automatic provenance captures direct reuse more readily than inspiration. The user control and expression family lets people act on the material: Plume can lock text while it regenerates the explanation around it [74]. The collaboration and perspective family makes interpretations available to other people: Wikibench supports discussion that revises label definitions and inclusion rules [69].

To use the taxonomy, start from a decision the person must make. Find the mechanism that supplies information or an action for it, then ask what response it requires and which outcome would show success. A provenance link, for example, gives a basis for checking a claim, but the person still judges whether the source supports the wording. The link shows traceability; accurate checking, or learning to judge sources, needs its own observation.

5.2 Mechanisms across workflows and years

GenAI control steers generation rather than correcting output. GenAI papers more often describe user control and expression (+13.7 points after adjusting for year and venue; 95% CI 8.6 to 18.7; Appendix D.2). In the 2,532 papers with facet codes, two control facets show a reliable gap, and both put generated candidates before the person: GenAI systems more often generate alternatives to explore (+4.8; 95% CI 3.0 to 6.6) and complete or continue the person's own content (+3.0; 1.4 to 4.6; Figure 9). The work people keep leans the same way, toward steering the loop (+3.4; 1.2 to 5.6) and away from improving the system (-5.9; -7.7 to -4.0; Figure 7). Acting on the output and stating criteria are not more common: editing machine output (+1.8; -1.4 to 5.1), direct manipulation of a semantic object (+0.9), and specifying criteria and rubrics (-2.8; -4.9 to -0.8). A choice among generated alternatives still needs criteria and contrasts, which few of these interfaces ask people to state (4.4% of GenAI papers). Section 4.2 and Section 5.3 compare designs that supply them.

GenAI systems rank items less often. Organization and comparison is less common in GenAI papers (Figure 10). Its largest facet gap is ranked or prioritized surfacing, which orders items so the important ones come first (3.2% of GenAI and 11.2% of traditional AI/ML papers; -6.5; 95% CI -8.3 to -4.7), and no other facet in the family differs by more than 2.9 points. Appendix D gives the annual family profiles (Figure 57).

Collaboration and perspective became more common over time.

Holding the technology mix fixed at the original analysis's reference composition (43.75% GenAI), its average annual change was +1.10 percentage points (95% CI [0.52, 1.68], Holm p=0.005). The 2023–2025 sensitivity also showed an increase (+2.67 points per year, CI [1.20, 4.14], Holm p=0.007). Guidance and feedback increased in the primary window (+1.58 points per year, CI [0.70, 2.47], Holm p=0.008), but its recent interval included zero ([-2.73, 6.47]). None of the five tests of change in the GenAI–traditional AI/ML difference survived Holm correction in either window. These temporal estimates (Figure 11) answer a different question from the overall technology-group differences in Figure 10; Appendix D.3 reports both temporal estimands for every family.

From task intent to action.

Mechanisms can also be grouped by the activity they support: specify intent, represent possibilities, evaluate alternatives, and act and revise (Figure 12). Appendix C.1 maps all 110 facet codes to these activities; a code can serve several. Annotations, histories, shared views, and handoffs connect the activities across time and people. The functions describe dependencies, not a fixed order: comparing needs alternatives and criteria, and a comparison may prompt a change to either.

Different mechanisms can serve the same function. Intent elicitation, constraints, and shared criteria frame a task. Structured alternatives and source links make possibilities inspectable; comparisons, explanations, and reflection support judgment; selection, editing, and changed constraints enable action. One mechanism can serve two functions: a comparison exposes options and supports choice, and a constraint can frame a task or redirect it. Guidance can enter at any point, and histories keep context across transitions.

Luminate's dimensions organize alternatives for exploration and evaluation, with return paths to earlier prompt-specific spaces [122]. AI Chains instead feeds one step's output into the next step's input, so people can inspect, edit, and re-run intermediate steps [139]. The order in which a system computes need not dictate the order in which people inspect or repair its work.

An ordered workflow can still require return paths. CollabCoder opens shared comparison after independent coding, then supports discussion, decisions, and grouping while letting people restore their original codes [45]. Crystalline instead builds a route back into the material: a reminder marks related evidence on pages the developer has visited but not yet attended to, and three of twelve participants reported using it to guide their research [75]. CollabCoder sets an order for the work; Crystalline returns people to an earlier step when their comparison may have a gap. Transitions therefore deserve the same design care as individual mechanisms: keep the criterion that shaped an alternative, the evidence behind a draft, and a route back to an earlier decision, and test whether people understand a transition, change it, and recover its context.

5.3 Revision, preservation, and control

An editable step does not guarantee that people can correct it and keep the later work they still want. Across the cases, the design question is what a human action authorizes the system to reuse or treat as accepted. Table 1 distinguishes saving an old version, preserving valid edits during regeneration, and confirming a result.

Keeping an old version does not carry its edits forward. Kazemitabaar et al.'s data-analysis systems saved earlier versions in branches, but regeneration ignored later manual edits [61]. Participants described avoiding revisions and expecting to redo or reread work; one wanted invalidated parts highlighted instead of regenerated, and another valued the interconnected updates. Recovering an old version differs from preserving the still-valid parts of that work in a new one.

LineageD's pilot showed the cost of predicting a whole lineage at once: correcting one pairing invalidated the rest of the path. The redesign predicts one level at a time, but moving to the next level implicitly confirms pairings the person has not individually confirmed [50]. Plume keeps locked or manually edited text and uses it as context for later generation [74], so a lock preserves wording without limiting its influence on other text or vouching for its correctness. Relating a local step to the whole process is hard in itself: in AI Chains, four of twenty participants asked how a local change would affect the final result [139].

Interfaces promise to keep different things. Automatic propagation can itself help. CoPrompt participants valued automatic coordination, and eight used history and difference views to resolve conflicts or restore versions [38]. Pail's code differences, summaries, and design panel supported inspection, but participants reported difficulty following cascades across them, less so when they paused to read the changes [143]. Selecting part of an artifact does not by itself fix what stays unchanged: FusAIn leaves unselected image regions untouched, whereas Textoshop can change text beyond the selected passage [103, 86]. Blace keeps earlier states for rollback, and DesignManager records the process behind an asset [78, 142]; both support recovery and inspection of past work, while consistency with a revised goal still requires checking the downstream artifacts. A design should name the property it protects and the change that could violate it, and an evaluation should test whether people anticipate that change, detect a violation, and recover the work they want to keep.

Edits can change the specification, the model, or the output. A correction can change what the person asked for, how the system understood it, or what it produced. FusAIn lets designers compose and revise a visual specification [103], and Falx synthesizes candidate charts from examples, which participants described checking against input values they knew [129]. CoAutoML lets novices inspect and edit the task, inputs, target, and evaluation assumptions it proposes before they confirm a machine-learning task [121]. Plume's locks retain part of what the system produced [74]. Outside generative chat interfaces, corrections can also update the model: SmartEye uses a corrected crop as a positive training example for later recommendations [82], and DeepSI fine-tunes BERT from spatial feedback and recomputes its document map, though its authors note limited visibility into the model's internal state [13]. The design question is what a correction changes and which later operation uses it, not whether every control comes before generation.

Generating alternatives and their criteria.

When a system generates the criteria as well as the alternatives, people must judge both. In Luminate, selecting an axis rearranges the responses, whereas adding a dimension revises the responses themselves [122], so the writer in our opening example judges the dimensions as well as the ideas. VIVID generates expected answers and rubrics along with candidate dialogues, and instructors inspect and edit them [29]. Design-rationale research already links questions, options, and criteria [84], and conventional tools sort alternatives into categories that designers choose. Generated criteria raise a narrower question: can people revise a criterion while holding the alternatives fixed, or does the revision also replace what they are judging?

Generated criteria can improve comparison. Selenite gives readers generated overviews of criteria and labels the relevant passages; in a twelve-person paired comparison with unaided reading, participants produced more valid criteria with the overview (12.93 versus 6.79), with higher precision and recall [76]. A criterion can also be easy to act on and still miss the quality it stands for. RECAST lets people revise text against a toxicity model; revisions lowered the model's toxicity scores without reliably improving human ratings of toxicity [137]. When both the model's response and human judgment matter, the evaluation has to measure both.

A label can also leave the question itself ambiguous. In a prior sensemaking study (Stream 2), an unexplained “trust” lens led some researchers to consider a person's trustworthiness and another to consider that person's trust in sensor data [35]. The same displayed criterion can therefore invite different judgments; understanding its use requires following what people take it to mean.

5.4 Comparing explanation and practice designs

Explanation content, required reflection, dialogue, and optional recommendations change different parts of practice. Table 2 links four AI-involved comparisons to their assessed outcomes.

The practice cost of reflection does not explain every null learning result. In Xiaomai's advanced-mathematics study, requiring error reflection produced neither a detected learning advantage nor a detected difference in attempts [37]. Together with the fixed-time comparison above, this makes the content and uptake of reflection worth examining alongside the practice it displaces.

Explanation design also concerns sequence. Incremental XAI supplies factors progressively during model-prediction practice, then tests prediction on unseen cases without the explanation display [16]. This separates the presentation of an explanation from what a person can do once it is removed.

Prior learning research separates creating an explanation from using it. In a randomized study of 120 learners, everyone wrote subgoal labels; those who then practiced with their own labels scored 21.6 of 25 on an immediate test, against 17.1 with expert labels and 18.8 with none. Instructional materials were removed for the test, while the programming environment remained available [85]. This comparison sharpens ExPeerience's question (Section 4.2): which part of the task should the person learn to perform? Learning research has long stressed what support asks learners to do [107, 28]; the interface choice is what to generate and what to leave for the learner.

NoteCopilot makes the amount of supplied structure a concrete comparison. In its thirty-person, within-person study, intermediate assistance yielded higher immediate understanding scores than either minimal or automated assistance when learners first answered without their notes [27]. The packages changed both the supplied material and the work of organizing it. This supports examining the division of work, without identifying engagement as the cause or establishing a delayed benefit.

Writing feedback can describe a revision or judge its quality. ArgRewrite classifies the purposes of a writer's earlier revisions without judging their quality, and asks writers to agree or disagree with those labels before and after revising again [1]. ArgueTutor pairs claim and premise labels with recommendations based on their balance [128], and LegalWriter adds advice on argument components while leaving the semantic fit between claim and conclusion to the writer [133]; both improved the quality of text written with them over their comparison interfaces. A description of a revision and advice about quality make different assertions, and one interface can offer both. A learning claim needs a test of the judgment or revision skill the feedback is meant to build.

5.5 How prior knowledge informs design

Prior knowledge enters a design through the material it supplies, the activity it asks of a person, and the measures used to assess it. The following cases trace those connections: making a relation visible, choosing an activity to observe, and carrying evidence from an earlier task into a new design.

The source-use map (Figure 14) links the wider lineage analysis to its recorded passages. It covers 2,058 papers, including the separate non-AI comparison set, and 51,815 source-use records; a source used by two papers counts twice. Readers can follow those connections on the companion website.

Making correspondence inspectable. Kori turns the concern about split attention into a visible link between prose and chart marks [71]. The system proposes links, and authors preview, accept, discard, or draw them by hand; once a link is accepted, hovering over its phrase highlights the chart marks it refers to (Figure 13). The author checks each correspondence, and the reader uses it to interpret the data.

Operationalizing a theory is not testing learning. QuizBot cites ICAP [28] as its learning rationale, whereas the Khanmigo methodology turns ICAP into an LLM-judged indicator of cognitive engagement [110, 125]. Deeper use of the theory does not bring stronger evidence of learning: QuizBot tests recognition two months later, while Khanmigo tracks correctness on the next item a student attempts alone. A direct test in diagnostic reasoning makes the distinction sharper: problematizing elicited more constructive responses than structuring, yet no condition advantage on diagnostic strategies was detected in subsequent cases after the pedagogical module was removed [47]. Both groups received active scaffolds, and the tests occurred in the same session. A theory can identify a promising activity; observing more of it still leaves its contribution to capability to be established.

Prior knowledge can shape the evaluation as well as the design. Sibyl adopts Doshi-Velez and Kim's application-grounded evaluation [152, 34], testing explanations with screeners in child-welfare work. Screeners often rated case-specific explanations helpful and found other forms less useful during those cases, and their feedback exposed problems of terminology and presentation.

A theory's evidence travels with its comparison. Codigen cites cognitive mapping to motivate active learning and supplies generated programming material on an editable whiteboard [36]. The cited medical study compares maps with notes organized around the same five problem-solving elements, with the assigned support available during the diagnostic case [131]. It does not compare self-authored with generated material. Codigen's novice pre/post quiz gains likewise do not isolate the whiteboard's contribution. The connection suggests a design, while testing its learning rationale would require comparing how learners construct and use the material.

Supplied material can support learning through its use. Learners need not build the material they learn with. VocabEncounter supplies phrases in context and reports better vocabulary two days later than its word-only condition [5]. Rehearsal supplies conversational alternatives, practice, and feedback; its participants used more cooperative strategies in a later unaided conversation than participants given the same static materials without interactive practice [114]. In a study of AI assistance for incidental learning, explanations without a recommended answer improved immediate concept learning over minimal feedback [43]. Supplied material also leaves room for different uses: CoNotate participants reported both running its suggested queries and borrowing their vocabulary to write new ones [98]. The design question is which operation the supplied material helps people perform, and whether the study tests that ability.

5.6 What capability the evaluation establishes

Three questions help interpret the comparisons: what did people do, how good was their work, and what could they do on a subsequent attempt? The process, artifact, and learning framework (Table 3) records those targets alongside the comparison, timing, assistance, and method of assessment. It distinguishes observed or externally assessed outcomes from self-report. Rating a finished artifact later still measures that artifact, rather than what its author has learned.

Product and capability measures answer different questions. In BELVEDERE, the maps showed more explicit links between evidence and hypotheses, but no difference in final prose conclusions was detected between conditions, and students could still consult their maps while writing [123]. Both outcomes describe products made with support; neither tests what students can do without the maps.

A benefit depends on the comparison and the situation. Cognitive forcing asks people to engage more deliberately with AI advice. Among 199 participants, fully correct decisions averaged 35% with simple explanations and 33% with forcing, a nonsignificant difference; on items with incorrect AI advice, forcing raised correctness from 3% to 9%, while the no-AI condition reached 18% [20]. Adaptive help raises the same issue: predicting whether a person will answer correctly differs from showing that advice based on that prediction helps them [120, 80]. Appendix A.7 gives the learning and duration profiles of the reviewed studies.

Assistance also defines the capability being tested: independence from a helper can coexist with continued use of a device. We return to that design choice in Section 6.3.

5.7 Performance and subsequent capability

An interface can improve one assessed outcome while leaving another unresolved. Table 4 distinguishes comprehension, revision quality, enacted behavior, and application of supported skills.

These comparisons apply Norman's distinction between performance with an artifact and the capability attributed to the person [94]. DBox's decomposition and feedback also improved performance on an immediate similar problem solved without assistance, although effort rose [81].

Assessment conditions specify the capability demonstrated. Among the 396 AI-involved sources in the outcome appraisal, 223 reported a separate capability assessment, 31 assessed capability in a later session, 71 used new material or a changed task, and 67 reduced or removed a named training aid. These overlapping features describe the selected appraisal set (Appendix A.8).

An assessment's task, timing, and available support each change what it shows: an immediate new problem can test application without testing retention, and a later test can still allow help. WriteAid tested pupils' writing two to three weeks later without AI or teacher support, but on the same topic and without an untreated comparison or a pretreatment skill measure [93].

The promised use determines the informative test. Immediate performance, later retention, and application to new material need not move together. Two classroom experiments with structured LLM reflection found no significant advantage on exams two weeks later [68]. Preference is not capability either: across three AI Margin Notes studies of reader interfaces, note selection, and human and AI note-taking, comprehension two hours after reading did not differ significantly, even where preferences or task demands did [59].

An informative evaluation therefore starts from the design's intended use. An explanation meant to prepare a new decision needs a decision task; feedback meant to change the next attempt needs that attempt observed; a practice partner meant to build interpersonal skill needs evidence of enacted behavior, while recall answers a different question. Effectiveness reviews already show that scaffolding can improve cognitive outcomes [11]; the comparisons here show which alternative and which outcome a designer can use as evidence.

Explore prior knowledge: reference map and documented source uses →

6 Discussion

Semantic scaffolding changes more than the amount of help a tool provides. It gives people material to think with, a way to judge that material, and particular work to do themselves. The findings support three positions: people need to be able to question the structure a tool supplies; evaluations need to distinguish better work from learning; and useful support can remain as people become more capable.

6.1 People need to judge the scaffold as well as its output

An AI tool can propose both an answer and the grounds for judging it. Luminate generates dimensions for comparing ideas; VIVID generates rubrics and expected answers alongside candidate dialogues [122, 29]. This can make a difficult comparison more tractable: Selenite helped readers identify more valid criteria [76]. But a usable criterion can still be a poor account of the quality people care about. In RECAST, reducing the model's toxicity score did not reliably improve human ratings [137]. The sensemaking study adds a semantic problem: the same “trust” label referred to different relationships for different participants [35]. People need to decide both what a criterion means and whether it captures the quality they care about.

Design rationale connects questions, options, and criteria [84]. Generative interfaces bring a new version of this problem into ordinary use: the system can compose the options and the criteria at the same time. People need to distinguish “Which option meets this criterion?” from “Is this the right criterion?” The interface can support that distinction by showing where a criterion came from, letting people compare different standards, and allowing them to revise a standard without automatically replacing the alternatives being judged.

Editing controls matter insofar as they make these choices practicable. Plume preserves selected wording during regeneration; the reviewed data-analysis systems can retain an earlier version while omitting its manual edits from regenerated work [74, 61]. A person reconsidering an assumption needs to see what that changes and keep work that still holds. Supporting that judgment means preserving valid contributions and making the consequences of a changed assumption inspectable.

6.2 Evaluate the work, its results, and what people learn

Three questions organize evaluation: what did people do, how good was the result, and what did they learn? The process, artifact, and learning framework in Table 3 keeps those questions distinct. Process evidence records actions such as checking, explaining, and revising, together with their time and effort. Artifact evidence concerns the resulting draft, program, or decision. Learning evidence concerns a person's capability on a subsequent attempt. Norman's distinction between the person–artifact system and the person's activity explains why success on one cannot answer the others [94].

The reviewed comparisons make the distinction consequential. CodeVoyager improved immediate closed-book comprehension without a detected advantage in assisted completion or accuracy; FeedbackWriter improved revisions without an established advantage on its optional knowledge test [63, 77]. Rehearsal improved enacted conflict-response behavior while recall and recognition advantages remained unestablished [114]. These are different benefits, and the appropriate learning measure depends on the capability the tool is meant to develop.

Observing the process helps explain the benefit and its cost. Required reflection displaced some practice within a fixed interval; QuizBot's equal-repetition comparison allowed substantially different practice times [7, 110]. In the algebra-video trial, optional uptake was low: the tested intervention was the offer of adaptive recommendations, not assigned video watching [70]. Evaluating all three questions means following the work people actually perform, judging its result, and testing the intended capability. It does not require one combined score or assume that more interaction produces more learning.

6.3 Support can remain while capability develops

Learning need not culminate in working without tools. Pea distinguishes scaffolding intended to fade from continuing distributed intelligence [102]; Krakauer asks what capability remains when an artifact's immediate advantage is removed [67]. Both direct attention to what the person gains. In vocational prompting, device-supported task correctness counted differently from asking a person for help [25]. The intended independence concerned human assistance, while the device remained useful.

This permits a deliberate division between useful automation and meaningful practice. Reiser distinguishes structuring a task from making its problems available for reasoning [107]. ExPeerience generates problem contexts and explanations while leaving SQL construction to the learner [149]. Rehearsal supplies a counterpart and feedback while the person practices responding [114]. Generating material can create an occasion for human activity as well as replace one. Designers should choose which capability deserves practice, then arrange the surrounding support to make that practice possible. The test is whether people become better at the chosen activity, with the resources their future work will actually provide.

7 Research Opportunities

The review opens four questions for research: which parts of a scaffold people should construct themselves, which activities account for learning, how judgments develop across people in real work, and how everyday tools can make room for learning. Each calls for studying a particular design choice rather than treating semantic scaffolding as a single intervention.

7.1 Decide which parts of a scaffold people should construct

AI can supply a comparison, a plan, or a rubric almost immediately. The design question is how much of that structure to provide and what to leave people to construct. Supplying criteria can help people notice distinctions they would otherwise miss, as in Selenite [76]. Constructing or revising criteria may instead engage people in deciding what matters. This is a concrete instance of the assistance dilemma: support can make progress possible while also taking over an activity the person needs to practice [66, 107].

Compare the same alternatives under three designs: supplied criteria, criteria people can revise, and criteria they construct with access to examples or feedback. Hold the alternatives fixed so that revising the standard does not also regenerate the objects being judged, as can occur when adding a dimension in Luminate [122]. Vary prior expertise and the stage of work. Examine which relevant distinctions people notice, how they justify a choice, and whether they can build a useful comparison on a new case. The aim is to learn when ready-made structure enables judgment and when participating in its construction is itself the valuable activity.

7.2 Identify which activities help people learn

An interface often bundles an explanation, practice, feedback, and extra time with the material. When a study finds a benefit, which of those made the difference? QuizBot's comparison held repetitions constant while practice time differed substantially; required reflection consumed some of a fixed practice interval [110, 7]. These comparisons motivate studies of what people do with support, beyond whether one interface package outperforms another.

The diagnostic-reasoning comparison shows why this matters: more constructive responses did not establish a subsequent strategy advantage [47].

Separate a focal activity from the rest of the interface: for example, compare seeing an explanation with predicting an answer before seeing that same explanation. Keep the task content, available help, and feedback comparable. Test equal-time and equal-repetition conditions where the activity changes the amount of practice. Observe uptake and reasoning, assess the work produced, and test the intended skill on new material immediately and after a delay. For optional support, distinguish the effect of offering the feature from the self-selected behavior of using it [70]. This would test whether adding the activity improves the intended skill under each practice budget, and whether gains persist on new cases with the resources available in ordinary use.

7.3 Study how people form and share judgments in use

Interactive systems offer a way to study how reasoning develops around a representation. Luminate makes proposed criteria available for revision; CollabCoder brings individual interpretations into shared discussion [122, 45]. Distributed cognition provides a basis for following the work across people and representations [49]. Observe when people adopt a criterion, contest it, or carry it into a later decision, and examine how deadlines and the demands of producing an artifact shape those choices. Interface traces need observation and participants' explanations to reveal why a judgment changed.

Handoffs make this question especially concrete. Compare a coaching summary alone with the same summary carrying the learner's priorities, evidence, and open questions, allowing equal preparation time [55, 17]. Follow what the coach infers, what the learner corrects, and which issues shape the next meeting. Analyze the coach–learner group together; assess learners directly when the claim concerns their learning. The opportunity is to understand which representations help people maintain and repair a shared interpretation as work moves between them.

7.4 Create learning opportunities within everyday tools

Tools for getting work done could also offer people opportunities to develop capabilities they want to retain. An explanation before a decision, a comparison between alternatives, or feedback on a proposed revision can make a moment of ordinary work available for practice. Incidental-learning research found an immediate concept-learning benefit from explanations without a recommended answer, compared with minimal feedback [43]; ExPeerience illustrates how generated material can leave the target activity with the learner [149]. These cases motivate embedding opportunities to reason within work, instead of treating learning only as a separate training phase.

Develop this approach around a capability chosen with the user: recognizing a misleading comparison, judging a source, or repairing a program. Offer a brief prediction, explanation, or correction at a relevant decision, with control over when to participate. Compare the ordinary tool with this added opportunity over repeated use. Assess interruptions, work quality, uptake, and later performance on new cases; remove the learning prompt while retaining resources that normally belong to the task. The central question is whether meaningful practice can fit the user's work well enough to support both present goals and growing capability.

8 Limitations

Coverage.

We searched 40 venues over 8 years, which favors published, English-language research [6, 73]. Technology comparisons leave out 639 papers whose AI technology could not be determined, and each analysis uses the papers coded for its fields (Table 9). The theories and empirical studies we compare against are a selection, not a census of every relevant tradition.

Reading and coding.

Language models read each paper against a fixed codebook, one model per paper, and grouped the coded descriptions into categories. People have not yet checked the coding or the cross-case interpretations. Models can miss evidence shown only in figures and can share biases, and other analysts could draw the boundaries between closely related mechanisms differently.

Effects.

Studies differ in tasks, participants, comparators, outcomes, and duration, and many compare whole systems. Most coded changes in how people work rest on the authors' own attribution rather than a measured contrast (75.8% of coded process shifts). The GenAI and traditional AI/ML comparisons are associations among published designs, not effects of the technology. The design space cannot rank mechanisms by effectiveness or estimate an overall learning benefit.

9 Conclusion

AI tools increasingly supply the structures people think with: criteria, examples, plans, and records of earlier choices. Our design space maps these semantic scaffolds across domains and connects each to the work it organizes and to what studies found. Generative-AI papers more often concern producing artifacts and include user-control mechanisms. What people can change matters, whether a specification, the AI's interpretation, the criteria, or the result, and support can reach a learner through peers, teachers, and coaches. Supplied material can support learning through the way people use it, and added interaction does not by itself make people practice the intended skill. The design space gives researchers concrete alternatives for building help that develops capability as people work, including the capability to use support that stays.

Appendix A Evidence Extraction and Coding

This appendix holds what a reader needs to check or reuse the coding: the fields of each evidence card, how the closed and open fields were coded, the agreement checks, the data behind each analysis, how sources for the outcome comparisons were chosen, and how cited sources were matched.

A.1 Card Fields

Each Stream 1 paper has a mechanism card (Table 5), and 2,058 papers also have a theory-lineage card (Table 6); each Stream 2 source has a knowledge-claim card (Table 7). The sectioned layout follows Model Cards [90], and AI-assisted design-card generation is a precedent for turning source findings into cards [118].

A.2 Closed Fields

Closed fields take values from a fixed list. Intent records whether the support targets immediate performance or sensemaking, learning or skill development, or both. Measurement records what the evaluation assessed, so an intention to support learning stays apart from a measure of it; the direction of a result and its observation horizon are recorded with the measure. Support properties are coded separately and can co-occur: structuring, problematizing, contingency, adaptation, fading, responsibility transfer, and distributed support. Contingency responds to the person's activity or need. Fading reduces support as competence grows; a fixed reduction on a schedule is not by itself fading. Responsibility transfer concerns who performs or regulates the activity, not whether the interface remains available. Technology is classified once per paper, from the AI in its system, an experimental condition, training, or evaluation, so a paper classified as generative AI can still contain mechanisms that involve no generation.

A.3 Open Fields

The 21 open fields hold 142,877 observations in the papers' own terms. Equivalent descriptions within a field were merged into 1,290 codes, and the codes were grouped into 223 categories and 92 families across 18 fields, with subcategories only where they add a distinction. Each grouping keeps links to its observations, and fields are never pooled. Codes that record missing information, such as an unspecified baseline or an unreported measure, stay apart from substantive categories. When one free-text value lists several limitations, its single code summarizes them rather than listing each. Appendix B defines the families and categories of the six fields the framework uses.

A.4 Agreement Checks

To test the open-code grouping, a separate model pass coded extracted observations with the existing codes hidden, and we compared the two groupings field by field (Table 8). An observation entered the comparison only when its identifier, source card, and field value matched exactly. Two codings need not use the same words, so we compared partitions: whether each pair of observations shares a code in each coding. The adjusted Rand index (ARI) corrects pair agreement for chance, and positive-pair F1 summarizes overlap among the pairs either coding groups together; neither treats one coding as correct.

Raw agreement is high because both codings keep most pairs apart: for facet, 19,083 of 19,503 pairs are apart in both and 32 are together in both. The blind pass used fewer codes than the existing coding in five fields and more in learning evidence. It reported medium or high uncertainty on most assignments in five fields (for example, 659 of 695 values) and on 7 of 24 in learning evidence. The learning-evidence row covers 24 of 48 existing observations; the other 24 share a repeated not-measured value and fell outside the comparison's selection rule.

A separate check asked only whether AI was involved: three fresh model sessions labeled 532 title-and-abstract records added in September and gave the same label to 529 (99.4%; κ=.988).

A.5 Validation Status of the Readings

For part of the evidence, the records of the original reading runs have not been fully validated, and we mark that evidence for provisional use. On 26 September 2026, such evidence appeared in 319 of the 1,076 learning papers and 1,252 of the 4,086 papers behind the main figures. The counts mark incomplete validation records, not errors, and the marked papers stay in the analyses.

A.6 Data Used for Each Analysis

Each analysis uses the papers coded for the fields it needs (Table 9).

All 2,847 open-coded papers have complete domain and retained-work codes; 532 lack complete facet–value codes. The closed-field population includes 44 papers outside the open-field profile and two with unresolved support-property coding.

A.7 Learning Measurement

Among the 2,891 closed-field papers, 301 (10.4%) measured learning. Two-thirds of those (199, 66.1%) measured it within a single session; 35 used repeated sessions, 38 followed people over weeks, and 25 measured learning in deployed use.

A.8 Selection of Sources for Outcome Comparison

The study comparisons in Section 5 draw on sources chosen for their outcome evidence. A learning-scope assessment of 4,714 records proposed 1,226 within scope. We appraised the 422 of these whose cards recorded that learning was measured (twelve more had been appraised earlier and were analyzed separately), plus 14 performance cases found among 53 descriptions that needed interpretation: 436 records, or 434 distinct PDFs. The 190 sources flagged as having a documented capability comparison entered the detailed synthesis.

A.9 Source Matching and Coverage

A.9.1 Source-use coding

Each theory-lineage record links one cited work to its role in one citing paper's design, argument, or measure (Section 5.5), so a work cited by two papers yields two records.

A.9.2 Citation metadata

The bibliographic map joins the two streams by DOI or Semantic Scholar paper ID and counts a paper found in both once. It uses Semantic Scholar data retrieved on 9 September 2026 for 4,331 Stream 1 papers and 448 Stream 2 works (28 in both). Reference lists for 3,233 papers name 106,523 cited sources; two with conflicting identities are withheld. Of the remaining 106,521, 5,748 are cited by at least five review papers and 157 by at least 40 (Figure 15). A reference list shows that a paper cites a work; its lineage card shows how the paper uses it.

The co-citation map counts each citing paper once per source and keeps sources with at least five citers and pairs with at least three shared citers. It weights a pair by association strength: the pair's shared citers times the number of papers, divided by the product of the two sources' citer counts. Louvain clustering (seed 42) forms the neighbourhoods, and a maximum spanning forest supplies the drawn links; stem, branches, and leaves mark how widely a source is shared. Less-cited sources sit near their most shared neighbourhood without joining it. The interactive atlas supports zooming into a neighbourhood and inspecting each source.[note]Interactive citation atlas: the interactive citation atlas.

A.9.3 Matching and unavailable sources

Cited works without a DOI are matched by title and year. Title variants can split one work into several identities, which overcounts distinct works and undercounts shared references; descriptive labels and conflicting identities stay out of the shared-reference map. Papers without a reference list, and full texts we could not obtain or read, are outside the source-use analysis.

Daggers identify absent or unspecified values, as defined in each row.

C.2 Complementary Evidence Profiles

The learning-by-family matrix uses the open-code classification and its 2,761-paper matched population. It is distinct from the closed-field learning count of 301 among 2,891 included papers.

C.3 Context and Evidence Profiles

The 2,891 closed-field papers record 2,071 empirical, 691 artifact, 123 methodological, four dataset, and two theoretical contributions. Contribution labels do not identify research methods or target users; study designs and participants are reported in Section 4.2.

In the design space, the domain mix shows no simple annual shift: technical, analytic, and creative professions account for 54.8% in 2019 and 55.5% in 2025, ranging from 53.4% to 61.6% across these years. Annual totals also reflect reading coverage and the incomplete 2026 publication window, so they do not estimate field-wide growth.

Study design is recorded for 2,071 papers: 691 within-subject designs (33.4%), 328 single-condition usability studies (15.8%), and 119 field deployments (5.7%). The 2,072 entries include one paper with two designs; percentages use papers. Usability studies reveal practical difficulties; deployments can expose work missed by short comparisons.

The participant field also covers 2,071 papers: mixed groups account for 540 (26.1%), target practitioners 499 (24.1%), and crowdworkers 251 (12.1%); 382 (18.4%) are unspecified. Participants need not represent a system's intended users, and missing descriptions do not establish broad applicability.

C.3.1 Most process shifts rest on an author's attribution

Of 8,045 process shifts across 2,891 papers, 6,102 (75.8%) are author-attributed, 1,746 (21.7%) use measured contrasts, and 197 are reviewer inferences. Baselines also differ: 1,940 use a control condition, 869 state none, and the remainder refer to prior practice or an author's assertion. Describing a changed workflow does not establish its effect size.

Appendix D Annual Trends and Venue Rates

These tests and counts support the comparisons in Section 4 and Section 5. Trends use AI-involved papers with usable codes for each field. Technology follows the AI a paper builds or uses, independently of publication year: generative AI includes hybrids and earlier neural generators; traditional AI/ML includes predictive, discriminative, and symbolic systems. The technology projection covers 3,447 classified papers; 639 remain unassigned. Each annual percentage uses papers with assigned technology and usable coding for that dimension in the same year. Count summaries combine 2019–2026; the annual lines separate the years. Alias disagreements are withheld for the affected field. Adjusted contrasts account for publication year and venue as described below.

D.1 Research-context trends

We model binary context membership with year and venue fixed effects, using venue-clustered standard errors with a finite-sample correction and Student's t reference distribution. The linear probability coefficient estimates average within-venue change in percentage points per year. Holm adjustment controls the family-wise error rate across the 16 directional tests. Intervals are pointwise 95% confidence intervals. Separate categorical-year tests check temporal variation and departures from a straight trend; these are available with the analysis data. Results describe the coded review frame.

D.2 Technology comparisons

We compare binary code membership using a linear probability model with technology, categorical publication year, and venue fixed effects. Primary estimates use 2019–2025, and sensitivity models restrict the analysis to 2023–2025 or add partial 2026. Venue-clustered standard errors use a finite-sample correction and a Student t reference with one fewer degree of freedom than the number of venues, and model intervals are pointwise 95% confidence intervals. Holm correction covers all 51 context, activity, family, and category contrasts jointly, with each sensitivity window and venue omission corrected separately. We omit six major venues one at a time: CHI, CSCW, EMNLP, IUI, TVCG, and VIS, each of which supplies at least 5% of the coded papers for workflow, families, or categories in 2019–2025. The choice rests on coding denominators, not outcomes. Weighting checks reweight shared year–venue cells with at least one or at least five coded papers per technology by pooled paper count, within-cell overlap, equal cells, equal venues, or equal years. Intervals for equal-venue gaps come from 10,000 resamples of venues.

User control.

User control and expression occurs in 633/1,071 GenAI papers (59.1%) and 623/1,373 traditional AI/ML papers (45.4%) in 2019–2025. Omitting each major venue gives gaps from +11.9 to +14.3 points, each with Holm-adjusted support (Table 13). On the 2,022 papers in shared year–venue cells, the gap is +12.5 with overlap weights and +7.8 when venues receive equal weight. Every weighting and cell threshold leaves it positive.

Facets and work codes.

The facet and work-code gaps in the main text use the same model on each paper's latest coding, with a normal reference for intervals. Of the 2,988 technology-classified papers from 2019–2025, 2,532 have facet codes (1,143 GenAI and 1,389 traditional AI/ML), 2,119 have codes for delegated work, and 2,526 have codes for the work people keep. Holm correction runs across the 101 facets coded on at least 40 papers and, separately, across the 24 work codes on at least 30 papers. A gap gets a direction in the text only if it has Holm-adjusted support, keeps its sign under all five weightings at both thresholds, and has an equal-venue interval that excludes zero at one threshold or both (Table 13 and Table 14). Fitted separately for the two models that coded most papers, the control gap is +13.9 (95% CI 8.8 to 19.0; 2,160 papers) and +11.1 (-1.1 to 23.3; 203 papers).

D.3 Temporal change in mechanism families

We distinguish average annual change in family prevalence from annual change in the GenAI–traditional AI/ML difference. Both come from a linear probability model with technology, publication year, their interaction and venue fixed effects. Average change holds the technology mixture fixed at 43.75% GenAI (the original primary cohort's reference share), separating it from shifts in the composition of the corpus. Positive gap change means movement toward a more positive GenAI difference; it need not enlarge the absolute gap. Venue-clustered intervals use finite-sample correction and a Student t reference. Holm correction covers all ten tests within each window; the 95% confidence intervals are pointwise. These are linear summaries of coded design prevalence, not tests of learning or causal technology effects. Partial 2026 is excluded.

D.5 Learning overlays

These counts cover the 3,378 papers with usable category coding, of the 4,086 papers in the analysis at 26 September 2026, including papers without an assigned AI technology. Learning scope means the paper is in the learning review; measured means the paper measured learning explicitly. Learning scope and Measured are counted separately within each category; missing or conflicting labels are omitted from the corresponding column.

Appendix E Vocabulary Growth During Reading

These curves show how each vocabulary grew as cards were read, so a reader can judge how complete the codes are. The vocabulary built from the first 3,295 mechanism cards gained 12 codes across the next 1,754 papers, and each new code was assigned to an existing category and family. All open fields were checked on 821 of those papers; the other batches checked mechanism facets, values, and domains (Figure 59).

E.1 Reading the Curves

We count distinct values after each batch of ten cards, in reading order, and scale each curve to its own final vocabulary. Codes, categories, and families are drawn where those levels exist; categories and families were assigned after coding, so they can reach their final size early in a curve. Reference lists in the lineage cards are open-ended, while their relation options are fixed by the card format. A flat segment means that no new label appeared in those cards, not that unread papers would add none.

E.2 Stream 1 mechanism cards: Interface and Outcome Fields

These grids show the variation the overview hides. Every panel states its field and final count, and lines are drawn only for the levels present in that field.

E.3 Stream 1 theory-lineage cards: Cited Sources and Their Roles

The curve covers the 1,952 newly written lineage cards; reused cards appear in the gallery but not in this sequence.

E.4 Stream 2: Claims and Conditions

Stream 2's seven open fields cover 542 cards and 35,699 observations. Of the 449 codes, 448 are used, and no new code entered in the last 16 coding batches. A flat curve can still hide a missing code: no population code names a studied unit that is or includes a machine, and 18 assignments flag this while using codes for people or artifacts.

E.5 New Codes Within the First Coding

Within the first coding of each open field, the last new code appeared between 2.5% and 48.7% of the way through the fields whose coding order was kept (Figure 63). Three fields still have low-confidence assignments for more than a quarter of their observations, so a vocabulary can stop growing and remain too coarse.
